quiz.question: A service inserts keys uniformly at random. Why does a classic B-tree usually pay more disk writes per insert than an LSM tree?
quiz.optionA: Each insert can dirty a leaf page (and maybe split), forcing an in-place random page write
quiz.optionB: B-trees rewrite the entire tree on every insert
quiz.optionC: LSM trees never fsync and therefore never write
quiz.optionD: B-trees store every key in two copies by design

quiz.question: What is the memtable + WAL pair actually buying you in an LSM store?
quiz.optionA: Faster range scans than reading SSTables
quiz.optionB: A durable crash-recovery log plus a sorted in-memory buffer so acknowledged writes survive a crash
quiz.optionD: A way to skip bloom filters on point lookups

quiz.question: Why might a single LSM point lookup inspect several SSTables?
quiz.optionA: Keys are hashed into random files with no order
quiz.optionB: The newest version of a key can live in any of several files produced over time
quiz.optionC: Bloom filters require reading every file
quiz.optionD: The WAL must be scanned on every lookup

quiz.question: On an LSM point lookup, what does a bloom filter actually tell you?
quiz.optionA: The exact file offset of the key
quiz.optionB: The key is definitely not in this SSTable, or it might be
quiz.optionC: Which compaction level owns the key

quiz.question: Why are LSM range scans of a key span often heavier than the same scan on a B-tree?
quiz.optionA: LSM trees cannot iterate keys in sorted order
quiz.optionB: You must merge iterators across the memtable and many overlapping SSTables
quiz.optionC: Range scans always replay the WAL

quiz.question: What happens when a memtable fills under normal LSM operation?
quiz.optionA: The process blocks until the next restart
quiz.optionB: It is frozen, flushed as an immutable SSTable, and a new memtable takes writes
quiz.optionC: All older SSTables are deleted immediately
quiz.optionD: The WAL is discarded before the flush finishes

quiz.question: Write amplification in an LSM tree is dominated by which activity?
quiz.optionA: Bloom-filter false positives
quiz.optionB: Rewriting the same live data again during compaction

quiz.question: What does read amplification usually mean for an LSM point get?
quiz.optionA: Bytes written per user write
quiz.optionB: How many disk reads or files you may touch to serve one user read
quiz.optionC: The size of the WAL in bytes

quiz.question: Why do B-trees typically win on short range scans of nearby keys?
quiz.optionA: Leaf pages keep keys in sorted on-disk order with little file overlap, often with sibling links
quiz.optionB: They never split pages
quiz.optionC: They attach a bloom filter to every leaf
quiz.optionD: They keep all data only in memory

quiz.question: What is compaction's main job in an LSM engine?
quiz.optionA: Increase write amplification for its own sake
quiz.optionB: Merge SSTables, drop obsolete versions and tombstones, and bound how many files a read must check
quiz.optionC: Turn the LSM tree into a B-tree
quiz.optionD: Disable the WAL after the first flush

quiz.question: After a crash, how is a lost memtable reconstructed?
quiz.optionA: Replay the WAL to rebuild in-memory state
quiz.optionB: Scan every SSTable for the newest key
quiz.optionD: It cannot be recovered; those writes are gone

quiz.question: A bloom filter returns a false positive for a missing key. What is the user-visible effect?
quiz.optionA: The engine returns a wrong value
quiz.optionB: An extra index/data read of that SSTable that then correctly reports the key absent

quiz.question: Why can LSM ingest a flood of random keys faster than a B-tree of similar durable settings?
quiz.optionA: User writes append to WAL and memtable instead of randomly updating leaf pages
quiz.optionB: LSM engines never fsync

quiz.question: Why does making flushed SSTables immutable matter for concurrency?
quiz.optionA: Old files can still be mutated in place
quiz.optionB: Readers can use a file lock-free while a new file is being written elsewhere
quiz.optionD: The memtable can grow without bound

quiz.question: Leveled compaction vs size-tiered: which statement about amplification is the useful default intuition?
quiz.optionA: Leveled usually trades higher write amplification for lower read and space amplification
quiz.optionB: Size-tiered always has both lower write and lower read amplification
quiz.optionD: The two strategies have identical amplification; only file names differ

quiz.question: A B-tree update of a 100-byte row that lives in a 16 KiB leaf: what is the first-order write-amplification story?
quiz.optionA: You write ~100 bytes because only the row changes
quiz.optionB: You typically rewrite the whole leaf (and maybe ancestors on split), so amplification is page-sized not row-sized
quiz.optionC: Write amplification is always 1 because of WAL grouping
quiz.optionD: Only the bloom filter page is rewritten

quiz.question: You undersize bloom filters so the false-positive rate is high. What happens to LSM point-read amplification?
quiz.optionA: Nothing; bloom filters are only used in compaction
quiz.optionB: More SSTables are opened and their indexes probed even though the key is absent

quiz.question: Why can a B-tree still beat LSM on a point get even when LSM has bloom filters?
quiz.optionA: A well-cached B-tree often needs one leaf I/O (plus a few internal nodes), while LSM may still miss cache on several files
quiz.optionB: B-trees never touch disk

quiz.question: A write stall in an LSM engine is most often a symptom of what imbalance?
quiz.optionA: Bloom filters are too accurate
quiz.optionB: Flush/compaction cannot keep up with ingest, so memtables or L0 files pile up and writes are throttled
quiz.optionC: The WAL is too small to hold one record

quiz.question: During an LSM range scan, bloom filters usually help how much?
quiz.optionA: They eliminate almost all SSTables, same as a point get
quiz.optionB: Little or none: a range may overlap many files, so you still merge-sort those overlapping runs
quiz.optionC: They convert the scan into a hash lookup
quiz.optionD: They replace the need for a block index

quiz.question: Space amplification in LSM is high when…
quiz.optionA: Obsolete versions and overlapping runs have not been compacted away yet
quiz.optionB: Bloom filters use a few bits per key

quiz.question: Why is WAL + memtable not enough by itself for long-term LSM health?
quiz.optionA: The WAL already stores sorted SSTables
quiz.optionB: Without flush and compaction, recovery time, file count, and obsolete versions grow without bound
quiz.optionC: Memtables cannot hold more than one key
quiz.optionD: Bloom filters cannot be built from SSTables

quiz.question: A workload is update-heavy on a small key set. Which engine property should you worry about first for LSM?
quiz.optionA: B-tree leaf splits
quiz.optionB: Compaction must keep rewriting those hot keys, so write amplification and tombstone/version churn stay high

quiz.question: B-tree fragmentation after many random in-place updates mainly hurts which operation?
quiz.optionA: Point gets of a single cached key, which never touch leaves
quiz.optionB: Range scans and sequential prefetch, because leaf occupancy and locality drop

quiz.question: You flush tiny memtables very frequently. What is the likely first-order effect?
quiz.optionA: Lower write amplification because files are small
quiz.optionB: Many overlapping SSTables, worse read amplification, and more compaction work later
quiz.optionD: Range scans no longer need merge iterators

quiz.question: Why does a leveled LSM often bound point-read I/O to roughly one file per level (plus L0)?
quiz.optionA: Each level (except L0) keeps key ranges mostly non-overlapping
quiz.optionB: Only one SSTable exists in the whole tree
quiz.optionC: Bloom filters store the level number of every key
quiz.optionD: The memtable is searched instead of disk

quiz.question: A B-tree checkpoint/WAL design vs LSM WAL: what is the conceptual difference for user writes?
quiz.optionA: B-tree WAL protects in-place page mutations; LSM WAL protects memtable contents until flush
quiz.optionB: Only LSM uses a WAL
quiz.optionD: Neither needs a WAL if fsync is used on data files

quiz.question: You need both fast random writes and efficient large range scans. What is the honest tradeoff to explain?
quiz.optionA: LSM favors ingest; scans pay merge cost across runs. B-trees favor locality; ingest pays random page writes
quiz.optionB: One structure always wins both, so pick either
quiz.optionC: Bloom filters make LSM scans as cheap as B-tree scans
quiz.optionD: Compaction removes the need to think about scans

quiz.question: The RUM conjecture is useful when choosing B-tree vs LSM because it says…
quiz.optionA: You can independently minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification at once
quiz.optionB: You cannot simultaneously minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification; LSM and B-tree sit on different corners
quiz.optionC: Only RAM size matters; on-disk layout is irrelevant

quiz.question: Universal/size-tiered compaction is piling huge overlapping runs. Which read path degrades first, and why?
quiz.optionA: Point gets of hot cached keys in the memtable
quiz.optionB: Wide range scans, because merge iterators fan in across many overlapping files of similar size

quiz.question: You have a block cache that already holds most inner index blocks. Where should you spend the next RAM dollar for LSM point gets?
quiz.optionA: Always more bloom-filter bits, even if data blocks are never cached
quiz.optionB: It depends: blooms cut negative lookups; caching data/filter blocks cuts positive lookups. Measure miss types
quiz.optionC: Never bloom filters if any cache exists

quiz.question: A leveled compaction write-amp estimate of ~10 (level ratio ~10) is missing which operational multiplier?
quiz.optionA: WAL write, memtable flush, and extra L0→L1 work when L0 is unsorted/overlapping
quiz.optionB: Bloom-filter hash count

quiz.question: Prefix bloom / partitioned filters exist because of which scan vs get tension?
quiz.optionA: Whole-file blooms help point gets but not prefix/range existence checks; partitioned/prefix filters prune files for both
quiz.optionB: They replace compaction
quiz.optionD: They store the full key in RAM

quiz.question: Delete-heavy LSM with lazy tombstone compaction: what is the dangerous read-path failure mode?
quiz.optionA: Point gets return random keys
quiz.optionB: Scans and gets keep resurrecting work: they must overlay tombstones from newer files onto older versions until compaction drops them
quiz.optionD: Bloom filters start returning false negatives

quiz.question: Why can a copy-on-write B-tree (or CoW page engine) still lose the LSM ingest race under random writes?
quiz.optionA: CoW still tends to write page-granularity trees and can amplify through ancestors; LSM batches into sequential runs
quiz.optionB: CoW never writes a WAL
quiz.optionD: LSM never writes more than once

quiz.question: An LSM write stall despite spare CPU often means which resource is the real bottleneck?
quiz.optionA: Bloom-filter CPU hash time
quiz.optionB: Flush/compaction bandwidth or L0 file-count limits: ingest is gated on making room, not on user-thread CPU
quiz.optionC: Too many range-scan merge iterators on idle cores

quiz.question: You must pick a structure for a working set that fits in RAM but a dataset that does not. Which statement is the staff-level read of amplification?
quiz.optionA: If internal nodes/filters/hot leaves stay cached, B-tree point reads can be one I/O; LSM still pays multi-level filter/index misses on cold keys
quiz.optionB: RAM size makes on-disk layout irrelevant
quiz.optionC: LSM point reads become free because memtable holds the dataset
quiz.optionD: Write amplification disappears when the working set is cached

quiz.question: Why is naive size-tiered compaction prone to space-amp spikes right before a large merge?
quiz.optionA: A merge of similar-sized runs temporarily keeps old and new copies until the new file is installed
quiz.optionB: Bloom filters double on disk
quiz.optionC: The WAL is checkpointed into every SSTable twice

quiz.question: A key-value API with many overwrite-in-place small rows vs append-mostly events: how do you argue the engine choice?
quiz.optionA: In-place small-row OLTP often wants B-tree locality and cheap point/range; append-mostly ingest wants LSM sequential write and later compaction
quiz.optionB: Always LSM because write amp is lower in every workload
quiz.optionC: Always B-tree because compaction is impossible to operate
quiz.optionD: The choice only depends on whether you have a WAL

quiz.question: Merge iterator during an LSM scan must resolve duplicate keys. What is the correct recency rule?
quiz.optionA: Oldest SSTable wins because it was flushed first
quiz.optionB: Newest sequence/memtable-or-file generation wins, including tombstones that hide older values

quiz.question: You observe LSM read amp rising while write amp falls after switching compaction style. What did you likely just do?
quiz.optionA: Moved toward more aggressive leveling (more rewrite, fewer overlapping files)
quiz.optionB: Moved toward lazier tiered/universal merging (less rewrite, more overlapping runs)
quiz.optionD: Replaced blooms with a full in-memory index of every key

quiz.question: Why is fsync of the WAL not the same as fsync of SSTables for crash correctness?
quiz.optionA: WAL fsync makes the latest memtable mutations recoverable; SSTable fsync makes a flush durable so WAL can be truncated
quiz.optionB: Only SSTable fsync matters; WAL is a cache
quiz.optionC: Only WAL fsync matters; SSTables can be torn forever
quiz.optionD: Both are optional if bloom filters are used

quiz.question: What does the partition key actually control in Cassandra?
quiz.optionA: The on-disk sort order of rows inside a partition
quiz.optionB: Which node(s) own the data: it hashes to a token and thus a replica set
quiz.optionC: The consistency level of the query
quiz.optionD: Whether a bloom filter is used

quiz.question: What do clustering columns control?
quiz.optionA: Which datacenter gets the write
quiz.optionB: Sort order of rows within a partition on disk and in queries

quiz.question: Replication factor (RF) vs consistency level (CL): which statement is accurate?
quiz.optionA: RF is how many replicas store a partition; CL is how many replicas must respond for this read or write
quiz.optionB: They are the same setting with two names
quiz.optionC: CL decides where data is stored; RF decides how many acknowledgements you wait for
quiz.optionD: RF only applies to reads; CL only applies to writes

quiz.question: With RF=3, what does a QUORUM write mean?
quiz.optionA: All 3 replicas must acknowledge
quiz.optionB: At least 2 replicas must acknowledge (majority of RF)
quiz.optionC: Only the coordinator stores the write

quiz.question: Why can a hot partition ruin a Cassandra cluster even when total QPS looks modest?
quiz.optionA: One token/partition is owned by a small replica set, so those nodes take all the load for that key
quiz.optionB: Cassandra cannot store large partitions
quiz.optionC: QUORUM is disabled for hot keys
quiz.optionD: Bloom filters stop working on busy nodes

quiz.question: What is a tombstone in Cassandra?
quiz.optionA: A backup of a deleted SSTable
quiz.optionB: A deletion marker that must be stored and compacted away later so old values do not resurrect
quiz.optionC: A hint stored on a coordinator

quiz.question: What is hinted handoff for?
quiz.optionA: Speeding up range scans
quiz.optionB: The coordinator stores a hint when a replica is down, then replays it when the replica returns

quiz.question: Why is a full-table scan (ALLOW FILTERING / unbounded partition scan) a junior anti-pattern?
quiz.optionA: Cassandra cannot read more than one row
quiz.optionB: Data is partitioned by token; a cluster-wide scan fans out and can overwhelm many nodes

quiz.question: LWTs (lightweight transactions / IF clauses) are expensive mainly because they…
quiz.optionA: Skip the commit log
quiz.optionB: Run a Paxos-style round of agreement instead of a regular quorum write

quiz.question: What does repair (anti-entropy) try to fix?
quiz.optionA: Hot partitions by splitting tokens automatically
quiz.optionB: Replicas that have diverged because of missed writes, downtime, or missed hints
quiz.optionC: The need for a partition key

quiz.question: You write at CL=ONE and later read at CL=ONE. Why might you miss your own write?
quiz.optionA: Cassandra never reads your own writes
quiz.optionB: The read may hit a replica that has not received the write yet
quiz.optionC: ONE always waits for all replicas
quiz.optionD: Tombstones block all reads at ONE

quiz.question: Why should a partition not grow without bound (wide partition)?
quiz.optionA: Clustering order breaks after a few rows
quiz.optionB: Compaction, repair, caching, and reads of that partition concentrate work on one token and huge SSTable pieces
quiz.optionD: QUORUM cannot count replicas for wide partitions

quiz.question: The coordinator node in a write path is responsible for…
quiz.optionA: Storing the only copy of the data
quiz.optionB: Sending the mutation to the replica set and waiting for CL acknowledgements

quiz.question: If RF=3 and you choose CL=ALL, what availability tradeoff did you make?
quiz.optionA: You can tolerate one replica down
quiz.optionB: Any one replica down makes the request fail, in exchange for seeing all copies

quiz.question: For RF=3, why is write QUORUM + read QUORUM the classic 'strong enough' pairing?
quiz.optionA: It contacts every node in the cluster
quiz.optionB: W+R>RF so the read set and write set must overlap on at least one replica

quiz.question: You write QUORUM and read ONE. What consistency property did you give up?
quiz.optionA: Durability of the commit log
quiz.optionB: The guarantee that the read intersects the write quorum; you can read a stale replica

quiz.question: A query with no restriction on partition key but a clustering-column filter is slow. Why?
quiz.optionA: Clustering filters require LWT
quiz.optionB: Without a partition key, Cassandra cannot target a replica set; it must scatter or reject/filter broadly
quiz.optionC: Bloom filters only work on clustering columns
quiz.optionD: QUORUM cannot be used without clustering columns

quiz.question: Range deletes and TTL expiry create many tombstones. Which read is most likely to time out?
quiz.optionA: A point get of a live key in a tiny partition with no deletes
quiz.optionB: A slice scan that must walk and skip huge runs of tombstones before finding live rows

quiz.question: Why can hinted handoff not replace repair?
quiz.optionA: Hints only cover some missed writes for a limited window; they do not reconcile all replica divergence
quiz.optionB: Hints always corrupt data
quiz.optionC: Repair cannot run if hints exist

quiz.question: LWT on a hot partition is especially painful because…
quiz.optionA: Paxos storage is on a different cluster
quiz.optionB: Each LWT serializes competing proposers on that partition; hot keys queue behind in-progress rounds

quiz.question: LOCAL_QUORUM vs QUORUM in a multi-DC cluster: what did you change?
quiz.optionA: RF in every DC
quiz.optionB: You wait for a majority in the local DC only, not a cluster-wide majority, cutting cross-DC latency

quiz.question: A single huge partition with millions of clustering rows: which maintenance operation becomes dangerous first?
quiz.optionA: Schema agreement
quiz.optionB: Compaction and repair of that partition, which must stream/merge a massive contiguous piece of data

quiz.question: Read repair vs full/incremental anti-entropy repair: how should you think about them?
quiz.optionA: They are identical background jobs
quiz.optionB: Read repair may fix replicas touched by a query; anti-entropy repair walks token ranges to reconcile even cold data
quiz.optionD: Anti-entropy repair only runs on the coordinator's memtable

quiz.question: Why does Cassandra still need gc_grace-style delay before dropping tombstones?
quiz.optionA: To keep bloom filters warm
quiz.optionB: A replica that was down could otherwise resurrect deleted data after tombstones are gone
quiz.optionC: QUORUM counts tombstones as live votes

quiz.question: You model 'all events for a user' as partition=user_id, clustering=time. What hot-partition pattern should you expect?
quiz.optionA: Users are perfectly balanced by definition
quiz.optionB: Celebrity/hot users concentrate writes and reads on one partition and its replica set
quiz.optionC: Clustering by time spreads data across all tokens

quiz.question: A coordinator stores many hints for a down replica. What operational risk follows?
quiz.optionA: Hints improve read latency forever
quiz.optionB: Hint replay can storm the recovering node, and hints can expire so divergence remains until repair
quiz.optionC: The down replica is removed from RF automatically

quiz.question: Why is 'RF=3, CL=QUORUM, but NetworkTopologyStrategy with RF=3 in only one DC' a different failure domain than two DCs of RF=3?
quiz.optionA: It is not; RF is global
quiz.optionB: Quorum is computed from the keyspace's replica placement; one DC of 3 means a DC outage loses quorum, unlike per-DC RF=3 with LOCAL_QUORUM

quiz.question: An LSM-style memtable flush in Cassandra is most analogous to which cost you already pay in the storage engine?
quiz.optionA: Token hashing
quiz.optionB: Write path is fast sequential; later compaction and many SSTables create read amplification for that partition

quiz.question: W+R>RF is necessary but not sufficient for 'I always read my write' in Cassandra. Which extra caveat is staff-level?
quiz.optionA: There are no caveats if W+R>RF
quiz.optionB: Clock/last-write-wins, partial replica failures, digest mismatch paths, and CL computed per-DC can still yield surprising recency without LWT/SERIAL
quiz.optionC: Partition keys are not hashed when W+R>RF

quiz.question: You need linearizable compare-and-set on a counter-like row. Why is 'read QUORUM then write QUORUM' the wrong tool?
quiz.optionA: QUORUM cannot read counters
quiz.optionB: Two clients can both read the same value and both write; you need LWT/Paxos (or an external consensus) to serialize the RMW

quiz.question: A repair that misses a recently deleted partition (gc grace elapsed, tombstone dropped, replica was down) produces what?
quiz.optionA: A harmless no-op
quiz.optionB: Data resurrection: the stale replica's live data is copied back to others

quiz.question: Hot-partition mitigation via bucketing (user_id + bucket) changes which costs?
quiz.optionA: It removes the need for RF
quiz.optionB: Writes spread across tokens, but reads of 'all buckets' become scatter-gather and you reintroduce merge/limit logic in the app

quiz.question: Why can EACH_QUORUM writes be the right multi-DC choice even though they are slow?
quiz.optionA: They contact only one node
quiz.optionB: They require a quorum in every DC, so a DC that was partitioned does not silently accept a CL that later cannot be read locally

quiz.question: LWT cost is not just extra round trips. What local storage-engine cost also shows up?
quiz.optionA: Paxos state (promises/commits) is persisted per partition, adding writes, contention, and more compaction on that key
quiz.optionB: LWT bypasses memtables entirely
quiz.optionC: LWT stores a full cluster snapshot
quiz.optionD: LWT turns off bloom filters cluster-wide

quiz.question: Incremental repair vs a naive full repair: what failure mode are you trying to avoid?
quiz.optionA: Token-aware routing
quiz.optionB: Repeatedly streaming already-agreed ranges, overloading disks/network, and extending the window where unrepaired data can resurrect after tombstone GC

quiz.question: A coordinator chooses replicas for a QUORUM read. Why might it still do extra digest reads?
quiz.optionA: To hash the partition key again
quiz.optionB: To detect replica disagreement cheaply, then fetch full data and reconcile, which is a form of read repair work
quiz.optionD: Digests are only for hinted handoff

quiz.question: Dropping gc_grace to 'clean tombstones faster' after a mass delete: what must already be true?
quiz.optionA: Nothing; it is always safe
quiz.optionB: Every replica has received the deletes and repair has covered the ranges; otherwise dropped tombstones invite resurrection

quiz.question: Why is a monotonically growing clustering key that is also the only partition key a dual foot-gun?
quiz.optionA: It is the recommended time-series pattern
quiz.optionB: One ever-growing partition (hot + wide) lands on one token; time-series wants time in clustering and a bounded partition key (and often time buckets)

quiz.question: Hinted handoff during a rolling outage of two of three replicas at RF=3, CL=QUORUM: what happens to writes?
quiz.optionA: Writes succeed because hints count as quorum votes
quiz.optionB: QUORUM writes fail; hints are not a substitute for live acknowledgements, so availability drops until a replica returns
quiz.optionC: CL is automatically lowered to ONE
quiz.optionD: The remaining replica becomes RF=1 silently

quiz.question: You must explain why Cassandra's last-write-wins on conflicting replicas is not a substitute for LWT.
quiz.optionA: LWW always waits for Paxos
quiz.optionB: LWW picks a timestamp winner after the fact; concurrent RMWs can lose updates. LWT prevents the lost update by agreeing before commit
quiz.optionC: LWW and LWT are identical on the same partition

quiz.question: A staff review of a 'one partition per tenant, all rows clustered' multi-tenant design should flag what first?
quiz.optionA: CQL cannot filter clustering columns
quiz.optionB: Tenant size skew becomes hot/wide partitions; noisy tenants dominate compaction, repair, and replica CPU with no token isolation
quiz.optionC: RF cannot be greater than 1 for multi-tenant data
quiz.optionD: QUORUM does not work with clustering columns

quiz.question: When would you accept CL=ONE writes in production despite stale-read risk?
quiz.optionA: Always; QUORUM is never worth it
quiz.optionB: When the workload is write-availability-first, reads can tolerate staleness, and repair/hints/read-repair are operated as the reconciliation path
quiz.optionC: When you also need linearizable CAS
quiz.optionD: When RF=1 already, so CL does not matter and you still claim multi-replica durability

flashcards.question: Why does a random insert usually cost a B-tree a full leaf-page write?
flashcards.answer: The engine updates a key in place inside a fixed-size leaf. Durability means writing that whole page (and maybe split parents), so amplification is page-sized, not row-sized.

flashcards.question: What roles do the memtable and WAL play together?
flashcards.answer: The memtable absorbs sorted in-memory writes for fast ingest. The WAL records those mutations durably first so a crash can rebuild the memtable before the next flush.

flashcards.question: Why can one LSM point get touch several SSTables?
flashcards.answer: Flushes create new files over time. The latest version of a key may live in a newer file, so the engine checks memtable then potentially multiple SSTables until it finds the newest value or proves absence.

flashcards.question: What does a bloom filter guarantee on an LSM lookup?
flashcards.answer: If it says no, the key is definitely not in that SSTable. If it says maybe, you must read the index/data; false positives only waste I/O, they do not return wrong values.

flashcards.question: Why are LSM range scans heavier than B-tree range scans of the same span?
flashcards.answer: A B-tree walk follows sorted leaves with little overlap. An LSM scan must merge-sort the memtable plus every overlapping SSTable that might contain keys in the range.

flashcards.question: What problem does compaction solve?
flashcards.answer: It merges SSTables, drops obsolete versions and tombstones, and bounds how many files a read must inspect—at the cost of rewriting live data (write amplification).

flashcards.question: How is the memtable recovered after a crash?
flashcards.answer: SSTables already on disk stay. The WAL is replayed to reconstruct unflushed memtable writes, then normal flush/compaction can continue.

flashcards.question: In one sentence, contrast LSM write amplification vs read amplification.
flashcards.answer: Write amplification is extra bytes rewritten (WAL, flush, compaction) per user write. Read amplification is extra files/I/Os touched per user read.

flashcards.question: How do leveled vs size-tiered compaction typically trade amplification?
flashcards.answer: Leveled keeps key ranges disjoint per level, lowering read/space amp but rewriting more (higher write amp). Size-tiered/universal merges similar-sized files, writing less often but leaving more overlap for reads and scans.

flashcards.question: When do bloom filters stop helping?
flashcards.answer: On wide range scans (files overlap the range anyway) and when the false-positive rate is so high that you still open most SSTables. They help negative point lookups most.

flashcards.question: What causes an LSM write stall?
flashcards.answer: Ingest outruns flush/compaction: too many memtables or L0 files. The engine throttles or blocks writers until compaction makes room, even if user-thread CPU is idle.

flashcards.question: Why can a cached B-tree still beat LSM on point gets?
flashcards.answer: Internal nodes stay in RAM, so a hit is often one leaf I/O. LSM may still miss on several per-file filters/indexes unless those are also cached and blooms are sharp.

flashcards.question: Why do tiny frequent flushes hurt later reads?
flashcards.answer: They create many overlapping SSTables. Point gets and especially range scans fan out across more files, and compaction must later rewrite that mess.

flashcards.question: What is space amplification in an LSM?
flashcards.answer: Live data plus obsolete versions, tombstones, and temporary extra copies during merge. It stays high until compaction installs the new file and drops the old ones.

flashcards.question: B-tree WAL vs LSM WAL: what is each protecting?
flashcards.answer: B-tree WAL (or equivalent redo) protects in-place page mutations until checkpoint. LSM WAL protects memtable contents until they are flushed to an SSTable and that file is durable.

flashcards.question: For update-heavy small key sets on LSM, what dominates cost?
flashcards.answer: Compaction keeps rewriting the same hot keys and their old versions. You pay write amp and tombstone/version churn even though the logical dataset is tiny.

flashcards.question: How does the RUM conjecture frame B-tree vs LSM?
flashcards.answer: You cannot minimize read, update, and memory/space amplification together. B-trees lean toward cheaper reads/locality; LSM leans toward cheaper updates/ingest; each inflates the other dimensions.

flashcards.question: You have RAM for either extra bloom bits or extra block cache. How do you choose?
flashcards.answer: Measure miss type. Extra bloom bits cut SSTable probes on negatives. Cache helps positive lookups and index/data blocks. There is no universal winner.

flashcards.question: Why is 'write amp ≈ level ratio' an underestimate for leveled LSM?
flashcards.answer: It ignores WAL, flush (L0), overlapping L0→L1 compaction, and any rewrites from deletes/updates. Operational write amp is those layers multiplied, not just per-level merge.

flashcards.question: How must an LSM merge iterator treat duplicates and tombstones?
flashcards.answer: Newest sequence/generation wins. A newer tombstone hides older values until compaction drops both. Oldest-file-wins would resurrect deleted data.

flashcards.question: Why can CoW B-trees still lose the random-ingest race to LSM?
flashcards.answer: CoW still tends to copy page-granularity nodes and ancestors. LSM batches many random keys into sequential runs; it defers random I/O into compaction instead of paying it on the user write.

flashcards.question: Why do prefix/partitioned blooms exist?
flashcards.answer: A whole-file bloom only answers 'is this exact key maybe in the file?' Partitioned/prefix filters can prune files for prefix or range existence without merging every overlapping run.

flashcards.question: If write amp falls and read amp rises after a compaction-policy change, what happened?
flashcards.answer: You likely moved toward lazier tiered/universal merging: fewer rewrites, more overlapping runs. The inverse move (more leveling) raises write amp and cuts read amp.

flashcards.question: Why must SSTable fsync and WAL fsync both happen, at different times?
flashcards.answer: WAL fsync makes the latest acknowledged memtable mutations recoverable. SSTable fsync makes a flush durable so the WAL can be truncated; skipping either breaks crash correctness.

flashcards.question: Partition key vs clustering columns: who does what?
flashcards.answer: The partition key hashes to a token and chooses the replica set (where data lives). Clustering columns sort rows inside that partition on disk and in queries.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between RF and consistency level?
flashcards.answer: RF is how many replicas store each partition. CL is how many replicas must acknowledge this specific read or write before success.

flashcards.question: With RF=3, how many replicas is QUORUM?
flashcards.answer: A majority of RF, so 2. ALL would be 3; ONE would be 1.

flashcards.question: Why are hot partitions dangerous?
flashcards.answer: All reads/writes for that key hash to the same token and the same small replica set. Those nodes become the bottleneck even if the cluster average looks fine.

flashcards.question: What is a tombstone and why must it exist?
flashcards.answer: It is a deletion marker stored like data. Without it, an older SSTable could resurrect a value after a delete. Compaction removes tombstones only after it is safe.

flashcards.question: What is hinted handoff?
flashcards.answer: If a replica is down, the coordinator may store a hint and replay the mutation when the replica returns. It is a short-term miss buffer, not full repair.

flashcards.question: Why are LWTs more expensive than ordinary writes?
flashcards.answer: IF / CAS uses a Paxos-style agreement round on the partition instead of a regular quorum write, adding round trips and contention.

flashcards.question: What does repair fix that normal reads/writes might miss?
flashcards.answer: Replica divergence from downtime, dropped hints, or missed mutations. Anti-entropy compares token ranges and streams missing data.

flashcards.question: Why does write QUORUM + read QUORUM with RF=3 give a replica overlap?
flashcards.answer: W+R>RF (2+2>3), so the set of replicas that took the write and the set that serve the read must share at least one node holding the data.

flashcards.question: Why can hinted handoff not replace repair?
flashcards.answer: Hints cover some missed writes for a limited time and can expire. They do not walk all token ranges or fix every kind of divergence. Repair still required.

flashcards.question: Why do tombstone-heavy slice queries time out?
flashcards.answer: The replica must scan and skip deletion markers to find live rows. Huge tombstone runs burn CPU/I/O and hit tombstone-failure thresholds before returning data.

flashcards.question: LOCAL_QUORUM vs QUORUM in multi-DC: what latency did you buy?
flashcards.answer: LOCAL_QUORUM waits for a majority in the local DC only, avoiding cross-DC round trips. Cluster-wide QUORUM may wait on remote DCs.

flashcards.question: Why must tombstones wait for a gc-grace window?
flashcards.answer: A replica that missed the delete could otherwise resurrect data once tombstones are gone. Grace gives time for hints/repair to propagate deletes first.

flashcards.question: Why is LWT on a hot partition especially bad?
flashcards.answer: Paxos serializes proposers per partition. Competing CAS operations on the same key queue behind in-flight rounds, amplifying latency far more than regular quorum writes.

flashcards.question: Read repair vs anti-entropy repair?
flashcards.answer: Read repair may fix replicas actually touched by a query. Anti-entropy repair walks ranges (including cold data) to reconcile the replica set systematically.

flashcards.question: What goes wrong with an unbounded partition (millions of clustering rows)?
flashcards.answer: Compaction, cache, repair, and reads concentrate on one token's huge contiguous data. Streaming and merging that partition can stall a replica.

flashcards.question: Why is W+R>RF not the same as linearizability?
flashcards.answer: It only argues replica-set overlap for a single write/read pair. Concurrent RMWs, LWW timestamps, per-DC CLs, and partial failures can still lose updates. Use LWT/SERIAL when you need CAS.

flashcards.question: What resurrection scenario must staff operators keep in mind?
flashcards.answer: A replica stays down past gc grace, tombstones drop, then repair/bootstrap copies the stale live rows back. Deletes vanish because the markers are gone.

flashcards.question: How does partition bucketing trade one problem for another?
flashcards.answer: user_id+bucket spreads writes across tokens (fixes hot/wide partitions) but reads of the full entity become scatter-gather with app-side merge/limit.

flashcards.question: Besides round trips, where does LWT cost show up in storage?
flashcards.answer: Paxos promise/commit state is persisted per partition, adding extra writes, contention on that key, and more compaction—not just extra network hops.

flashcards.question: Why can EACH_QUORUM be worth its latency?
flashcards.answer: It requires a quorum in every DC, so a DC that was partitioned cannot accept a write that the other DCs will never see, which LOCAL_QUORUM can allow.

flashcards.question: Do hints count toward QUORUM?
flashcards.answer: No. QUORUM needs live replica acknowledgements. If two of three replicas are down at RF=3, QUORUM writes fail; hints cannot vote in their place.

flashcards.question: LWW vs LWT for concurrent updates: what is lost without LWT?
flashcards.answer: Last-write-wins picks a timestamp after the fact, so two RMWs can both read the same base and one update disappears. LWT agrees on the CAS before commit.

flashcards.question: What is the first staff flag on 'one partition per tenant'?
flashcards.answer: Tenant skew becomes hot/wide partitions. A noisy tenant dominates compaction, repair, and replica CPU with no token isolation from others.
